parts.text: I’m searching the library for the DPDP public-data exemption and its limits for hiring.

input.query: DPDP publicly available data exemption section 3(c)(ii) self-published third-party tagged posts employment section 7(i) applicants accuracy Rules 2025

results.title: DPDP Act 2023, s.3(c)(ii): publicly available personal data
results.citation: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, section 3(c)(ii)
results.summary: The Act does not apply to personal data that the person it relates to has made, or caused to be made, publicly available, or that someone is legally obliged to publish.
keyPoints: The exemption turns on WHO made the data public: the person themselves, or someone under a legal obligation.
Content posted by friends or family that tags or names a candidate was not made public by the candidate, so it is not covered.
The Act does not define 'made publicly available', or say what happens when a post is later made private or deleted.
Public is not the same as exempt: scraping operations should not assume every visible post falls outside the Act.
results.caveat: The scope of the exemption is untested before the Data Protection Board. Whether a vendor's bulk collection for scoring is covered is an open legal question for Kestrel's counsel.

results.title: DPDP Act 2023, s.7(i): legitimate use for employment purposes
results.citation: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, section 7(i)
results.summary: An employer may process personal data without consent 'for the purposes of employment' or to safeguard itself from loss or liability, with examples such as preventing corporate espionage and protecting trade secrets.
keyPoints: Every statutory example is defensive and security-specific.
Commentators read it as not authorising blanket surveillance.
It refers to employment; whether it extends to applicants who are not yet employees is unsettled.
results.caveat: Whether s.7(i) covers social-media screening of applicants has not been decided. Legal counsel must take a view.

results.title: DPDP Act 2023, s.8(3): accuracy of data used in decisions
results.citation: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, section 8(3)
results.summary: Where personal data is likely to be used to make a decision that affects the person, the data fiduciary must ensure its completeness, accuracy and consistency.
keyPoints: A hiring shortlist is a decision that affects the candidate.
A profile matched to the wrong person, or a post misread by a model that does not understand its language, fails this duty.

results.title: DPDP Rules 2025: notification and phased commencement
results.citation: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 (notified 13 November 2025)
results.summary: The Rules were notified on 13 November 2025. Most operational duties — notices, security safeguards, breach reporting, retention — apply from 13 May 2027, eighteen months after notification.
keyPoints: Notices must give an itemised description of the personal data and the specific purpose.
Kestrel's 2027 hiring cycle will run after the main obligations take effect.

parts.text: I’m searching for necessity and less intrusive alternatives to assess whether social screening is proportionate.

input.query: Puttaswamy proportionality necessity less intrusive means hiring social media consent notice alternatives

results.title: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India: privacy and proportionality
results.summary: The Supreme Court held privacy to be a fundamental right and applied a proportionality test to intrusions: a legitimate aim, a rational connection to it, no less restrictive means that would work, and a fair balance between the aim and the intrusion.
keyPoints: The test binds the State; for a private employer it is the accepted Indian standard for judging whether an intrusion is justified.
Question 6 of this review — is there a less intrusive way? — is the necessity limb of the test.
results.caveat: Applied here as a normative standard. The constitutional test does not bind a private company directly.

results.title: DPDP Act 2023, ss.4–6: lawful grounds, notice and consent
results.citation: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, sections 4, 5 and 6
results.summary: Where the Act applies, personal data may be processed only for a lawful purpose, with consent or for a listed legitimate use. Consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, limited to the data necessary for the purpose, and preceded by a notice.
keyPoints: The notice must describe the personal data and the purpose, and how to withdraw consent and complain.
Consent covers only the data necessary for the specified purpose.
Consent in hiring is rarely free: a candidate who refuses fears losing the job.

results.title: US FTC: social media background reports are consumer reports
results.authority: Reference only: not binding in India
results.citation: FTC closing letter to Social Intelligence Corp., 9 May 2011
results.summary: The FTC treated a company compiling social-media reports for employers as a consumer reporting agency, bringing accuracy duties and the obligation to notify applicants of adverse action.
keyPoints: Social-media screening vendors carry accuracy and notice duties in the US.

results.title: Indian employers already screen social media
results.citation: CareerBuilder India survey of 1,200 employers, reported by People Matters
results.summary: 59% of surveyed Indian employers used social media to research candidates, a further 33% planned to, and about 68% of those who found negative content decided against hiring.
keyPoints: The practice is common in India; this review is about doing it at scale and by machine.
results.caveat: An older employer survey; current figures may differ.

results.caveat: Small sample; not a validation of any automated tool. Recorded so the review does not overstate the case against.

parts.text: I’m applying the decision rules to obtain the recommendation, permitted uses and matters reserved for people.

output.headline: Do not adopt as proposed. Orbis SocialFit should not be used to score or shortlist campus applicants.
rationale: 9 of 13 signals fail the review and must be removed; they carry 69% of the tool's scoring weight.
Under the vendor's configuration, 4 group comparisons fall below the 0.80 impact-ratio line: college tier, language of posts, religion (synthetic label), social media presence.
After the review, no signal is left in the automated score. Shortlisting falls back to Kestrel's own aptitude test, and no group falls below the line.
The vendor has not provided a validation study, so the claim of "92% accurate at predicting who joins and stays" cannot be checked. There is no evidence the tool predicts joining or retention.
1 signal raises a legal question only Kestrel's counsel and Data Protection Officer can answer.
permittedUse: Ask every candidate directly about further-study plans and joining date at offer stage, and record the answer. This replaces the higher-studies signal, which addresses Kestrel's real problem: offers accepted and not taken up.
Verify claimed projects and skills against LinkedIn or GitHub links the candidate supplies, as a pass-or-query check by a person. Never rank on it, and never penalise a candidate without a portfolio.

If Kestrel wants a conduct check, a trained person may review only content the candidate published themselves that shows explicit threats, harassment or hate, in a language they understand, with the candidate given the chance to respond.
Hold the competing-offers signal until the Data Protection Officer and counsel have decided whether it may be used at all.

gaps.text: Validation study linking scores to joining and retention (missing): Without it, the 92% accuracy claim cannot be checked, and there is no evidence the tool predicts anything.
Description of training data (missing): If the model learned from past hires, it can learn past hiring bias, as a well-known retail recruiting tool did.
Independent bias audit (missing): No selection-rate comparison by gender, region, language or college tier has been done.
Languages the text models support (partial): The vendor confirms English. Hindi, Hinglish and other Indian languages are 'in beta'.
Method for confirming a profile belongs to the candidate (partial): The vendor matches on name and photo similarity. No error rate was given.
Platform permissions for data collection (missing): Several platforms prohibit using their data for background checks or surveillance.
Data retention and deletion terms (partial): Reports are kept for 'up to 5 years' with no link to the hiring purpose.
The fairness test uses 1,000 synthetic applicants built on stated assumptions. It shows what the scoring rules do to a realistic mix of people, not what happened to real applicants.
The review assumes Kestrel's aptitude test treats all groups equally. That test was not audited here; if it is biased, falling back to it inherits that bias.

Mentions of other job offers: Whether reading candidates' posts about competing employers is covered by the DPDP publicly-available exemption, and whether penalising a candidate for considering other offers is acceptable practice for Kestrel.
Whether the DPDP exemption for publicly available data covers a vendor's bulk collection of candidates' posts for scoring is untested.

One small study (Kluemper et al., 2012) found trained raters' Facebook personality ratings correlated with job performance; a larger one (Van Iddekinge et al., 2016) found no link. Neither validates this vendor's signals.

humanDecisions.decision: Whether 'culture fit' should be scored at all for campus hires, and whether the offer-stage conversation is an acceptable substitute for prediction.
Whether any collection of candidates' social media is lawful under the DPDP Act, including the open question on the competing-offers signal.
The final decision on the proposal, recorded below with names, date and reasons.

decisionRules: D1. If removed signals carry more than half the scoring weight, the vendor configuration fails the fairness test, or no signal survives in the automated score: do not adopt as proposed.
D2. Otherwise, without a validation study: pilot with safeguards only.
outcomeRules: R1: If a signal stands in strongly or directly for a personal characteristic (question 2 fails), remove it.
R2: If a signal has no link to the job or to joining (question 1 fails), remove it.
R3: If a signal raises an open legal question, send it to a human decision-maker before any use.
R4: If a less intrusive method answers the same question (question 6 fails), restrict the signal and use that method instead.
R5: If the signal may read the wrong person, content others posted, or misread some groups (question 3, 4 or 5 fails), restrict it to human review under conditions.
R6: If three or more questions raise concerns, restrict the signal.
R7: Otherwise keep the signal, with a condition for every question that raised a concern.

parts.text:
## Recommendation

Do not adopt as proposed. Orbis SocialFit should not be used to score or shortlist campus applicants; this matches `getDecisionRules`.

## What I did

- Used `getCaseFile` to establish the problem, proposal and vendor-document gaps.
- Applied `getSignalReview` to all thirteen signals, then examined S02, S03, S04, S13, S05 and S07 individually against the six questions.
- Opened five fictional cases using `getCandidateReview`, checking identity, authorship, language, absence penalties and unfair uplift.
- Ran `runFairnessTest` under vendor and reviewed configurations.
- Made three `searchEvidenceLibrary` searches covering public-data exemption, necessity and predictive validity.
- Applied `getDecisionRules` and recorded five hand-offs using `recordHandoff`.

## What I found

Kestrel’s last cycle had 18% offer reneging and 22% first-year attrition. The proposal would screen about 55,000 aptitude-qualified applicants annually and exclude those below the social-score shortlist line.

| Signal | Tool outcome |
|---|---|
| S01 Late-night posting | Remove |
| S02 Slang and profanity | Restrict |
| S03 Higher-studies preparation | Restrict |
| S04 Other job offers | Needs human decision |
| S05 Party/alcohol photos | Remove |
| S06 Political/protest content | Remove |
| S07 Religious/festival content | Remove |
| S08 Followers/engagement | Remove |
| S09 Language of posts | Remove |
| S10 Employee-network overlap | Remove |
| S11 Engagement/wedding posts | Remove |
| S12 Little/no social media | Remove |
| S13 Professional-profile consistency | Keep, with conditions |

Nine removed signals carry 69% of scoring weight. S05 lacks job relevance and has identity/authorship failures. S07 directly tracks religion and lacks job relevance. S02 requires language-capable human review of explicit threats, harassment or hate, with candidate response. S03 must be replaced by direct offer-stage questions. S04 remains on hold. S13 permits candidate-supplied professional links, neutral treatment of absence and a response opportunity; it supplies no automated ranking points.

These are fictional diagnostic cases, not hiring recommendations:

| Sample | Failure pattern | Vendor → reviewed score |
|---|---|---|
| Arjun Verma | Hinglish cricket banter misread | 62.7 → 70 |
| Rahul Sharma | Wrong profile; no checked details matched | 59.4 → 74 |
| Dev Patil | Friend’s protest tag; Marathi misread | 61.1 → 67 |
| Kavya Behera | No-social-media penalty | 62 → 76 |
| Aditya Malhotra | Followers, English and connections inflated score | 88.2 → 60 |

Both fairness configurations selected 500 of 1,000 synthetic applicants.

| Flagged comparison | Vendor selection rates | Reviewed rates |
|---|---|---|
| College tier | Tier 1/2/3: 72%/55%/39% | 50%/50%/50% |
| Post language | English/Hindi–Hinglish/other Indian: 65%/47%/38% | 49%/49%/51% |
| Religion, synthetic labels | Majority/minority: 52%/40% | 50%/51% |
| Social presence | Active/minimal/none/private: 51%/54%/19%/55% | 50%/50%/49%/50% |

Vendor gender and region comparisons were unflagged. The reviewed configuration contains no social signals in its automated score and has no flags.

## What the evidence says

The DPDP exemption concerns data made public by the individual, caused by them to be public, or published under legal obligation; a friend’s tag is not automatically exempt [[1]](https://www.meity.gov.in/static/uploads/2024/06/2bf1f0e9f04e6fb4f8fef35e82c42aa5.pdf). Applicant coverage under employment legitimate use remains unsettled [[2]](https://www.barandbench.com/law-firms/view-point/navigating-legitimate-use-exemption-employee-data-digital-personal-data-protection-act-2023). Where applicable, decision data must be complete, accurate and consistent [[3]](https://dpdpa.com/dpdpa2023/chapter-2/section8.html).

The library reports most operational DPDP duties commence on 13 May 2027; implementation must account for phased commencement [[4]](https://www.hoganlovells.com/en/publications/indias-digital-personal-data-protection-act-2023-brought-into-force-). Puttaswamy supports necessity and less intrusive means as a normative standard here; its constitutional test does not directly bind private employers [[5]](https://globalfreedomofexpression.columbia.edu/cases/puttaswamy-v-union-of-india-ii/). Where DPDP applies, consent must cover necessary data and follow notice [[1]](https://www.meity.gov.in/static/uploads/2024/06/2bf1f0e9f04e6fb4f8fef35e82c42aa5.pdf).

Van Iddekinge found no predictive relationship with performance or turnover [[6]](https://digitalcommons.memphis.edu/facpubs/12063). Kluemper found positive correlations using trained personality raters in a small employed subsample; neither study validates SocialFit [[7]](https://www.hrreporter.com/news/hr-news/is-facebook-an-effective-screening-tool/314279).

## Gaps and limits

- **Missing:** Validation, training-data description, independent bias audit and platform permissions. The 92% claim is unverified.
- **Conflicting:** Research findings disagree and examine different methods.
- **Unclear:** Bulk-scoring exemption, applicant employment coverage, deleted/private posts; incomplete language support, identity-error rates and purpose-linked retention.
- **Outside my authority:** Legal determinations, business policy, approval and candidate decisions. Synthetic results do not prove fairness; group passes can hide individual harm. Aptitude fairness was assumed, not audited.

## Handed to people

- **Legal counsel:** Resolve exemption, applicant coverage, S04 and applicable Indian-law requirements.
- **DPO:** Decide lawful, proportionate processing and safeguards.
- **Head of Talent Acquisition:** Decide culture-fit policy, joining alternatives and treatment of competing offers.
- **Both owners:** Commission missing-evidence verification and aptitude audit.
- **Both owners:** Make and document the final decision.

## What Kestrel can do instead

Ask everyone about study plans and joining dates at offer stage. Verify candidate-supplied portfolios through human pass-or-query checks, without ranking or absence penalties. Use narrowly scoped, language-capable human conduct checks with notice and response. Hold S04 pending DPO and counsel determination.
